title: Device-Independent Self-Testing of the Three-Qubit CCZ Hypergraph State
authors: Yunguang Han, Xin Kuang, Xingyuan Bu, Yukun Wang
abstract: The three-qubit CCZ state is the smallest rank-three hypergraph state and an elementary entangled magic resource. Its cubic phase is governed by generalized stabilizers that are not Pauli strings, so standard graph-state self-testing arguments do not apply directly. We show that twenty correlators, all obtainable from five of the eight global input triples in the tripartite two-input, two-output scenario, determine this state and the action of the Pauli $X/Z$ measurements up to local isometries. The proof fixes eight equally weighted computational branches and propagates conditional $X$-flip relations across the branch cube, recovering the minus sign of the $111$ amplitude. These five-context correlations are nonlocal, but the canonical Pauli measurements cannot attain the largest quantum value of any Bell inequality that they violate: whenever they maximize a Bell expression, its local bound has the same value. Introducing an independent third measurement makes self-testing from maximal Bell violation possible. We construct an explicit Bell inequality whose maximal quantum violation self-tests the CCZ state and all three local measurements. An exact sum-of-squares decomposition proves the quantum bound, and its equality conditions yield an analytic SWAP extraction. Together, these results give two explicit device-independent self-tests of the CCZ state and demonstrate that determining a state and its measurements from several correlator equalities is distinct from identifying them through the maximal violation of a single Bell inequality.
summary: This paper develops advanced theoretical protocols to self-test the three-qubit CCZ hypergraph state in a device-independent manner. It shows that standard methods fail due to non-Pauli stabilizers, requiring the use of specific correlator equalities and constructing novel Bell inequalities for verification. The results clarify the distinction between determining a state from correlation constraints versus finding it via maximal quantum violation.
main_problem: The authors aim to develop device-independent self-tests for the three-qubit CCZ hypergraph state, addressing limitations of standard graph-state testing methods.
main_result: They provide two explicit device-independent self-tests for the CCZ state, demonstrating that determining a state from correlator equalities is distinct from identifying it via maximal Bell violation.
method: The work combines analyzing twenty specific correlators derived from five measurement contexts with constructing and proving bounds on an explicit Bell inequality using Sum-of-Squares (SOS) decomposition over algebraic number fields.
model_or_system: The system is the three-qubit CCZ hypergraph state, which serves as a resource for quantum information processing. The analysis focuses on its non-Pauli stabilizer structure and its behavior under local measurements.
key_observables: Correlators (input–output probabilities), Bell inequality violations, and generalized stabilizers ($K_A$).
important_parameters: The state is defined by the cubic phase polynomial; the test relies on comparing nonlocal correlations to local bounds (e.g., 11 vs 9).
main_assumptions: Standard graph-state self-testing arguments fail because the stabilizers are not standard Pauli strings, necessitating alternative mathematical tools.
figures_summary: The notes reference figures showing branch cube propagation and equations defining correlations (e.g., Table 1 listing measurement contexts).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing that correlator equalities fix the state to showing why maximal Bell violation fails for canonical measurements, culminating in the construction of a successful Bell inequality test.
why_interesting: This work provides rigorous mathematical tools (SOS proofs) to verify quantum states and measurement settings without trusting the physical device's perfect operation, which is crucial for scalable quantum technologies.
